title: Given an array of points on a plane and a value K, return the K points closest to the origin, where distance is Euclidean (the square root of x squared plus y squared).
shortTitle: K Closest Points to Origin: max-heap of size K by distance
keyPoints: Use a max-heap of size K keyed on squared distance; the farthest point sits on top for easy eviction
Compare squared distances instead of true Euclidean distances to avoid costly square roots and floating-point
Offer each point; when the heap exceeds K, poll the top (farthest) to keep exactly K closest
Time is O(n log K) and space is O(K), better than sorting all n points in O(n log n)
Use long for squared distance to avoid integer overflow on large coordinates
QuickSelect on squared distance is an alternative giving average O(n) time when all points fit in memory

s1_definition.oneliner: Use a size-K max-heap keyed on squared distance; offer each point and evict the farthest when size exceeds K, leaving the K closest in O(n log K).
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Max-heap of size K** – a priority queue that keeps the farthest point on top; when a closer point arrives and the heap exceeds K, the farthest is evicted.
- **Squared distance** – comparing x*x + y*y avoids the square root; squaring preserves ordering for non-negative values.
- **Time O(n log K)** – each of n points is offered to a heap of size at most K, so each offer is O(log K).
- **Space O(K)** – the heap never holds more than K entries.
- **QuickSelect alternative** – average O(n) time using the selection algorithm on squared distances.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India mobile app shows the K nearest ATMs to the customer's location. You keep a shortlist of K, ordered so the farthest sits on top. When you consider a new ATM, you add it and, if the list grew past K, drop the current farthest. The K that remain are the nearest.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Points: (3,3) (5,-1) (-2,4) (1,1) (-1,0)    K=3

  Squared distances from origin:
    (3,3)  -> 18
    (5,-1) -> 26
    (-2,4) -> 20
    (1,1)  -> 2
    (-1,0) -> 1

  Max-heap (farthest on top), cap at K=3:

  Step 1: offer (3,3)=18      heap: [18]
  Step 2: offer (5,-1)=26     heap: [26, 18]
  Step 3: offer (-2,4)=20     heap: [26, 18, 20]  size=3=K
  Step 4: offer (1,1)=2       heap: [26, 18, 20, 2] size=4>K
          poll top=26 (5,-1)  heap: [20, 18, 2]
  Step 5: offer (-1,0)=1      heap: [20, 18, 2, 1] size=4>K
          poll top=20 (-2,4)  heap: [18, 2, 1]

  Result: (3,3)=18, (1,1)=2, (-1,0)=1  -> K closest
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
K Closest Points to Origin asks for the K nearest points and the efficient solution uses a max-heap of size K ordered by squared distance, with the farthest point on top. I offer each point, and when the heap exceeds K I poll the top to remove the current farthest. After all points are processed, the heap holds exactly the K closest.

Comparing squared distances instead of true Euclidean distances is a deliberate choice. Squaring is monotonic for non-negative values, so it preserves ordering, and it avoids both the cost and the floating-point imprecision of square roots. I use `long` for the squared sum to prevent overflow on large coordinates.

The choice between a max-heap of size K and other approaches is what interviewers probe. Capping the heap at K bounds both memory and per-element cost at O(log K), which matters when n is large and K is small. QuickSelect gives average O(n) time but has O(n^2) worst case and requires all points in memory.

At the National Bank of India, the mobile app used this pattern to show the K nearest ATMs to the customer's GPS coordinates. The service scanned the ATM network once, held only K candidates in memory, and returned the nearest ATMs quickly without sorting the entire network or computing square roots.

Remember one sentence: a max-heap of size K keyed on squared distance finds the K closest points in O(n log K) time and O(K) space by evicting the farthest point whenever the heap overflows.
